patterns: Interactive sensory illusions that trick the viewer's visual or cognitive processing within seconds
Relatable anthropomorphic framing of daily brain functions (e.g., fatigue, focus, caffeine response)
Counter-intuitive neurological phenomena featuring sudden, surprising real-world trade-offs
Micro-visualizations of internal neural mechanics using simple everyday analogies (e.g., car brakes, filtering networks)
Ultra-concise high-concept visual demonstrations optimized for immediate loopability under 40 seconds
title_formulas: How Your Brain [Surprising Everyday Function] Without You Knowing
Why Your Brain [Unexpected Cognitive Habit] Under Stress
What Really Happens Inside Your Brain When You [Common Daily Action]
opening_3s: Display an immediate optical trick on screen and prompt the viewer to test their perception right away
Show a fast visual metaphor comparing a daily sensation to a mechanical lock or barrier inside the head
State a common mental habit and visually cut to a stylized neural map responding instantly
comment_themes: Appreciation for vivid, easy-to-understand physical metaphors and everyday analogies
Strong positive reaction to charming, expressive visual representations of psychological concepts
Humorous self-deprecating confirmation that their own mind experiences the exact same quirk
Curiosity about practical everyday applications for focus, learning, and daily habits
avoid: Exaggerated medical claims, dramatic injury shock-bait, or promising instant mental cures
Overly clinical, jargon-heavy lectures that lack immediate visual demonstrations or relatable metaphors
Intrusive ambient audio or overly alarming music cues that distract from simple educational clarity
try_next: A 30-second breakdown on the psychological illusion of attention based on early 20th-century perception studies, using a quick visual spot-the-change test
A 35-second visual metaphor exploring how memory consolidation works during sleep, framed as a librarian organizing index cards
A 40-second clip on why selective listening occurs under sensory overload, grounded in classic attention theories with a simple audio-visual exercise
